description: We are a team of 4 students from the American University of Bahrain, 2 Computer Science and 2 Multimedia & Design students ready to sonify the galaxy
summary: The Melodic Earth Jukebox is a multi-layered sonification project, converting six EIC visualizations of natural and man-made Earth characteristics (global temperature from 1880 to 2025, precipitation and clouds, lightning, city lights, CO₂ emissions and nitrogen oxides) into audio. Using a web app built with WebGL and Tone.js, the colors and light intensities in the EIC visualizations are read through NASA’s own color keys and mapped to notes of different pitches. Each visualization has its own instrument: natural characteristics play traditional instruments (cello, flute, violin) and man-made characteristics play synths, which slip off key where the data is strongest. Layering visualizations creates a harmony that shows how these factors combine and affect the Earth. The Jukebox makes EIC visualizations accessible to blind and visually impaired users through sound, screen-reader support, voice commands and a narrated story. Captions and haptic feedback extend access to deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and the multisensory experience makes EIC data easy to understand for everyone. Built by team Sonific-8 in Bahrain, it won Best Use of Technology at the Bahrain Riffa (Kingdom University) local event.
details:
What it does

Melodic Earth Jukebox is a web app that plays six NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations as one piece of music. The first page is a jukebox: each EIC map is a record with its own instrument. Pick records, press Play, and the jukebox slides away to reveal one shared map where the chosen records are stacked and playing.

Record (NASA SVS)

Instrument

What you hear

Global temperature, 1880–2025 (5603)

Cello

Warmer than 1951–1980 plays higher

Rain and clouds (5149)

Flute and clarinet

Heavier rain, more notes

Lightning (5011)

Violin

Each flash is a strike

City lights (5475)

Synth pad

Brighter cities play louder

CO₂ emissions (5121)

Deep synth drone

More carbon, thicker drone

Nitrogen oxides (5154)

Gritty synth

Dirtier air, rougher sound

How it works

Several times a second, the app reads each map’s current frame on a half-degree grid. Each pixel’s color is matched to the nearest color on that visualization’s own NASA color key, which gives a value from low to high. Those values become music at 80 beats per minute in one shared key: higher values play higher notes, more coverage plays louder and more often, and a sound’s position on the map sets whether you hear it in your left or right ear. Nature stays in tune. Humanity’s synths slip slightly off key where their data is strongest: the dirtiest air, the brightest cities, and the places that have warmed most.

There are three ways to listen. Listen plays everything on screen. Scan sweeps a needle across the map, and each point plays the moment it is crossed. Probe plays one spot, and a narrator says where it is and what each record shows there, such as “1.2 °C warmer than in 1951–1980”. Then and Now buttons let you hear temperature in 1880 and in 2025, and city lights in 2012 and 2023. A How it works view lets anyone drag along a color key and hear exactly which note each color becomes. A narrated story of about a minute and a half plays each record alone, zoomed into where its data is densest, then layers them together.

Benefits and intended impact

The World Health Organization estimates that at least 2.2 billion people have a vision impairment, and NASA’s maps speak only to people who can see them. Our app works without the screen: every control is labeled for screen readers, number keys pick records, voice commands work with or without holding a key, the story plays hands-free, and an Xbox controller vibrates with the sound, each record with its own feel. Captions describe the music for deaf and hard-of-hearing users. For sighted people it adds what a single map can’t: warming, storms and pollution experienced together, and the “Lighten our footprint” lever, which fades human activity out so you hear the planet with a lighter touch.

Tools, languages and hardware

TypeScript, React and Vite for the app; WebGL to stack the six maps on one map; Tone.js to play instruments our multimedia team recorded; Kokoro, an open neural voice, for narration; the Web Speech API for voice commands; the Gamepad API for controller vibration; Python and ffmpeg to download and prepare the NASA data; and GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages to publish it. Zoomed in, the base map streams NASA Blue Marble tiles from NASA GIBS. Code: https://github.com/hanawahban/sonific-8

Why it’s creative

It treats NASA visualizations as records you can mix, not pictures to look at. Nature and humanity sound different on purpose, acoustic against electronic, so the contrast is heard, not explained. The jukebox interface, designed by our multimedia team, makes it playful enough for a classroom and simple enough for a first-time user.

What we considered

Honesty about the data: we read the published visualizations, not raw science values. They are about 19 km per pixel; temperature is coarser, on NASA’s 2° grid. Each record keeps its real dates, from 145 years of temperature to recent days of rain, so layers line up in place, not in time. The app says so. We also checked our readings against NASA’s own numbers: the temperature map reads +1.2 °C for 2025, NASA’s published figure. Accessibility from the first design, not added at the end. Comfort: vibration is gentle and capped, and the music ducks under the narrator. And performance: small versions of the maps load first, so it starts quickly and runs smoothly on an ordinary laptop.
